perOption.reason: Direct contradiction of the thesis. The passage explicitly argues students should 'think through ethical issues rather than follow a prescribed set of ethical codes or rules' and that principles of conduct 'vary both between and within individuals'. A title asserting codes must remain strict and universal negates both the thesis and the supporting claims (formal contradiction: passage asserts variability and flexibility; option asserts fixity and universality).

Exact match at correct generality. 'Ethical Thinking' names the passage's topic term; 'Judging Issues' maps to 'identifying ethical issues and evaluating these issues from different perspectives'; 'Beyond Fixed Rules' maps to 'rather than follow a prescribed set of ethical codes or rules' plus the no-clear-right-or-wrong premise. The title subsumes both supports (inter/intra-individual variation, context dependence) without overreach. Grammatically well-formed as a title (NP: gerundive apposition).

Category error / misreading of the opening conditional. Critical thinking appears only as a definitional analogy ('If we understand critical thinking as..., then ethical thinking is about...') used to define ethical thinking, not to replace ethics. The passage argues FOR ethical thinking as a form of ethics ('This form of ethics is distinct from...'), so no replacement claim exists anywhere in the text.

Part-for-whole overgeneralization. 'Religious' occurs once inside a disjunctive enumeration ('social, religious, or civic beliefs') as one of several influences on personal values; no primacy ('core') claim is made, and 'training' is never discussed. Elevating one list member to the title's core claim is formally unsupported.

Double contradiction. The passage asserts (a) 'Individual perspectives may also be context dependent... the same individual may make different choices' (negating 'context-free') and (b) 'there is no clear right or wrong response' (negating 'one right choice forever'). The option is the logical negation of two explicit premises.

note: Title question with a clean single answer. Distractors are all formally refutable: 1 and 5 are direct negations of explicit claims, 3 misreads a definitional analogy as a replacement thesis, 4 inflates a single list item. Option 2 is the only candidate covering thesis + both supports at the right level of generality. No alternative charitable reading rescues any other option. Lens: grammarian/logician; all rejections anchored to quoted textual premises.
